title: Nonexperts Use the Wrong Criteria to Make Selections of Quality
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines a recurring pattern in organizational decision-making: when leaders make selections outside their area of expertise — choosing consultants, vendors, AI tools, creative products, or talent in domains they don't deeply understand — they systematically rely on the wrong criteria. Instead of assessing actual performance quality, nonexperts default to brand familiarity, social proof, visual polish, likeability, and short-term comfort, while giving too little weight to evidence of objective performance, established track record, and strategic fit. Research shows nonexperts also prioritize immediate outcomes over long-term effectiveness. The result is that low-quality programs and vendors become entrenched in organizations not through merit but through the misapplication of nonexpert judgment at decision points. The article is a warning to busy leaders who stray from their core domains: the decision criteria that serve them well as experts may be completely unavailable to them as nonexperts, and the substitutes their brains offer — brand, polish, popularity — are systematically misleading indicators of quality.
points: Brand familiarity, social proof, and visual polish are cognitively easy signals for nonexperts to interpret, which is why they dominate nonexpert selection decisions — and also why they are systematically misleading about actual quality.

Nonexperts ask 'does this feel right to me?' rather than 'is this good?' because feeling right is easier to defend in a meeting than objective performance evidence — and this substitution explains how mediocre programs become institutionally entrenched.

The short-term comfort vs. long-term effectiveness tradeoff is particularly acute for nonexpert selectors: ease of implementation feels like quality, but ease of implementation and instructional effectiveness are often inversely correlated.

The risk is systemic: when nonexperts make repeated selection decisions across an organization, the cumulative effect is an institutional ecosystem of 'feels right' choices that collectively undermine performance and are very hard to dislodge.

The practical implication for leaders is to identify explicitly which decisions fall outside their core expertise, and to build in deliberate mechanisms — expert consultation, evidence requirements, track record audits — before those decisions are made.
quotes: Many of an organization’s worst decisions aren’t made by incompetent people. They are made by smart, confident people who are nonexperts in the domain where they have decision-making authority.

They don’t decide wrongly because they ignore important criteria but because they give too much weight to superficial attributes, such as brand, social proof, and likeability, and too little weight to the performance criteria most important to true experts. Research reveals that nonexperts also prioritize immediate outcomes, such as short-term comfort and speed of implementation, over long-term effectiveness, established track record, and strategic fit.

Instead of asking, “Is this program or vendor good?” they ask, “Does this feel right to me?” They know that feeling right is much easier to defend in a meeting than being right. This is one reason so many low-quality programs, experts, and experiences are brought into organizations and become deeply entrenched over years.

For instance, when marketing experts make artistic decisions, or when human resources experts decide between artificial intelligence tools, they depend too heavily on what others are doing rather than doing the work to discern quality and performance. Busy leaders make the same poor decisions when they stray from their core expertise.

Of course, this leads to poor choices across any domain where they lack true expertise. Nonexperts are drawn to cues that are easy to interpret, like brand familiarity, visual polish, or social media reviews.

So, brand familiarity, visual polish, and social media reviews crowd out more objective measures of quality when they make decisions regarding which programs, people, and tools to bring into the organization. Over time, these weak choices can have a tremendously negative impact on the overall quality of the organization.

The tragedy is that it feels indistinguishable from good judgment to the person exercising it. A confident choice predicated on superficial criteria carries all the emotional weight of a well-reasoned one, which is precisely what makes it so dangerous.
